text: With the storage account standing, this lesson moves the actual product images into it -- creating a container, picking the right access tier, uploading the files, and pointing the app at their new home.

First, a container inside the storage account: product-images. It's a flat namespace, but the app's existing folder-like structure can still be part of each blob's name, and the portal displays it as folders even though the storage underneath stays flat.

The access tier is decided by one question: how often are these images actually read? Shoppers view product images constantly, every time a catalog page loads. That's the textbook case for the Hot tier -- highest storage cost, but lowest access cost and no retrieval delay. Cool or Archive would save a little on storage but add latency or an hours-long rehydration delay neither customers nor the launch deadline can afford.
upload-batch moves every file in the exported local folder into the container in one command, at the Hot tier -- the practical choice for hundreds of product photos instead of one at a time.

Moving the files is only half the job. Every blob has a predictable public URL built from the storage account and container name, and the app's image-rendering code gets updated to build URLs in that shape instead of the old local file path.

An upload command finishing without an error only proves the upload didn't fail. Real validation means three checks: a count check comparing blob count to source file count, a spot check that images actually load and look right, and an app check that the catalog app renders them correctly from the new URLs. Next lesson moves to the second half of the migration -- the VM workload itself.
